blocks.text: The account of Jerusalem’s siege, Jehoiachin’s capture, the installation of another king, and the removal of tribute has a near-contemporary Babylonian parallel in BM 21946, often called the Jerusalem or Nebuchadnezzar Chronicle. That record helps situate 2 Kings 24:8-17 within the political transition it narrates, while not extending to the later destruction of the temple.

The removal described here should not be read as the whole of Jerusalem’s later catastrophe. Kings and Jeremiah distinguish Jehoiachin’s removal, along with selected leaders and groups, from the later destruction of Jerusalem and further deportations under Zedekiah. Administrative tablets from Nebuchadnezzar’s palace also record provisions for a ruler identified as Jehoiachin, his dependents, and other Judeans, providing context for his continued recognition and maintenance in Babylon, though not confirming the later release scene in 2 Kings 25.
